# Library QC cell: one Waters LC-MS can't QC all 768 products within 24 hours in this model

With no more input available, I made a provisional design under the assumptions below. The model doesn't support the 24-hour target with your one Waters LC-MS, and none of my three designs reached it. These are simulation predictions, not measured performance.

## Assumptions (none came from you)
- **Scope:** synthesis, workup and purification happen before this cell. Each 96-well product plate arrives ready to sample. 8 plates × 96 = 768 products.
- **Timing (cautious case):** all 8 plates become available only when the last reaction finishes, so the whole QC must fit in 24 hours. The target is therefore 768 products/day, running 24 hours a day.
- **LC-MS method:** about 210 s per sample (range 120–360 s), so 20,160 s per plate, with no blanks or standards counted.
  - This is the catalog's estimate, not a vendor or measured figure.
  - The literature search found no library-QC cycle time I could cite. The closest result was a 4-minute run time in a serum bioanalysis paper (doi:10.1016/j.jpba.2024.116179), which is a different application, so I didn't use it.
- **Screening:** a 96-well fluorescence assay with a 1-hour incubation (a placeholder).
- **Room:** 7 × 5 m with one door.
- **Staff:** one technician on an 8-hour day shift.
- **Hazards:** flammable solvents and toxic reagents; the LC-MS sits in a ventilated zone.
- **Budget:** unknown, so the design is provisional.

## Design and results
The cell has input and output plate hotels and an Opentrons Flex. The Flex makes a QC plate and an assay plate from each product plate. QC plates go to the LC-MS; assay plates go through a PlateLoc sealer, a Cytomat incubator and a CLARIOstar reader, then to data review. UR5e arms move the plates.

| Version | Change | Throughput (products/day): P10 / P50 / P90 | Chance of meeting target | What limits it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | Baseline, Waters only, one arm | 146 / 192 / 192 | 0 | The liquid handler is out of the arm's reach, so the technician carries plates to the LC-MS during the day shift only. Waters busy 48% of the time. |
| v2 | Add a second UR5e arm | 280 / **384** / 498 | 0 | **The Waters is busy 99.9% of the time.** It is the hard limit. |
| v3 | Add an Agilent 1290/MSD iQ as a second LC-MS | 263 / 384 / 384 | 0 | The layout put both LC-MS units out of the arms' reach, so the technician has to load them. Each runs about 48% of the time. |

**v2 is the real answer to your question.** With one Waters running non-stop, the model's median is 384 products/day, half the target. At that rate the 768 products take about two days.

The target needs about 112.5 s per sample or less, all-in. Even the fastest end of the estimate (120 s) is too slow before adding blanks or standards.

v3 was my last allowed revision, and it didn't show that two instruments are enough. In the design, the second LC-MS has no robot feeding it overnight.

Simple arithmetic (not a simulation): two LC-MS units fed around the clock at 20,160 s per plate give a ceiling of about 823 products/day. That would only just clear the target at the central estimate and would fail at the slow end. Two-instrument feasibility is unproven.

## Checked claims
- **"P50 meets 768 products/day": refuted.** The verifier recomputed 384. I withdraw any suggestion that this design meets the target.
- **"Zero layout violations": refuted.** There is 1 violation: people hand plates into arm_2's reach at the liquid handler and output hotel, and the UR5e isn't rated for working beside people. A light curtain or a pass-through hotel would fix this, but neither is in the catalog. They're priced only as a placeholder of about $4k.
- No budget was given, so cost wasn't checked against one.

## Cost (catalog estimates, excluding installation, service and consumables)
- **v3 equipment list:** $611,352, including the Waters you already own ($156,700). That makes new spend about **$454,652**.
- **v2 (Waters only, two arms):** new spend about **$240,468**.

## What would change the answer
1. **Plates finishing one after another:** if plates finish in sequence, QC on early plates can start before the last reaction ends. Only the tail end would then need to fit in the 24 hours, and the target could be reachable with one instrument. This is the biggest unknown.
2. **A measured cycle time:** a real sample-to-sample time well under about 112 s, including blanks, would make one Waters possible in principle.
3. **A second LC-MS:** it would need to sit inside an arm's reach, with that arm's 24-hour operation simulated before you commit.

The report I generated matches these findings. Nothing here is a safety certification.

We need all 768 library products QC'd by LC-MS within 24 hours of the last reaction finishing, using the one Waters UPLC-MS we already own. Design the QC and screening cell around it.

Your previous reply was:
I'm not starting the design yet. The catalog estimate for your instrument suggests the 24-hour target may not be achievable with one LC-MS, so a few questions need answering first.

## Feasibility check from the catalog
- **Your instrument:** the catalog lists `waters_acquity_uplc_qda` (ACQUITY UPLC I-Class PLUS with QDa). It runs one sample at a time.
- **Run time per plate:** 20,160 s per 96-well plate, with a range of 11,520–34,560 s. That works out to about 3.5 minutes per injection cycle, with a range of 2–6 minutes.
  - This is an agent estimate (a short gradient plus injection and re-equilibration, times 96 samples), not a vendor or measured figure.
- **Your library:** 768 products is 8 reaction blocks of 96 wells. LC-MS time is per sample, so all 768 need injecting.

| Case | Time per sample | Total for 768 samples |
|---|---|---|
| Central estimate | 210 s | 161,280 s ≈ 44.8 h |
| Best case | 120 s | 92,160 s ≈ 25.6 h |
| Worst case | 360 s | 276,480 s ≈ 76.8 h |
| Needed for 24 h (86,400 s) | 112.5 s or less | 24 h |

These are simple lower limits on instrument time, not simulation results. They leave out blanks, standards, system-suitability runs and downtime, which would make things worse.

So whether one instrument can meet the target depends mainly on your real method and on when QC can start.

## What I need from you
1. **Real injection cycle time:** what is the full sample-to-sample time on your Waters method, including injection and re-equilibration? How many blanks or standards do you run per plate? This number decides feasibility, and if you have a measured value I'll use it instead of the estimate.
2. **When QC can start:** do the 8 blocks finish one after another, so early plates can go on the LC-MS before the last reaction ends? Or do all 768 become available only after the last reaction finishes, so the whole run must fit inside the 24 hours?
3. **What happens between reaction and LC-MS:** does each block go straight to QC, or through workup, filtration, purification or evaporation first? Is synthesis itself in scope, or only QC and screening?
4. **Screening assay:** what's the readout (fluorescence, luminescence or absorbance), plate format (96, 384 or 1536 wells), any incubation time, and do you need reformatting or compound storage?
5. **Room:** width and depth in metres, door positions, and any no-go areas.
6. **Budget:** in USD for new equipment, since the LC-MS is already owned. Or tell me I can go ahead with a provisional design without a budget.
7. **Operating hours and staff:** hours per day the cell runs, and how many operators work which shifts.
8. **Hazards:** I'll assume flammable solvents from the LC-MS and any evaporation, so the cell needs ventilation and separate solvent storage. Any toxic reagents, inert-atmosphere needs, or other hazards?
9. **Second instrument:** if one Waters can't meet the target, can I compare adding an instrument? The catalog has an Agilent 1290/LC-MSD iQ at about 150 s per sample (estimated, about $214k list price). Or must the design stay at one LC-MS and show the shortfall?

Once I have these, I'll build the layout and run the Monte Carlo simulation. I'll then check the results with the verifier: throughput against your target, cost against budget, and zero layout violations.

No more information is available, and nobody can answer questions. State your assumptions and give your best design, or say it can't be done and why.

lab_spec.name: 768-product library QC and screening cell (provisional)
lab_spec.description: All 768 library products QC'd by LC-MS within 24 h of the last reaction finishing, using the one existing Waters ACQUITY UPLC I-Class PLUS/QDa; design the QC and screening cell around it. User could not supply further details; provisional design with stated assumptions.
notes: ASSUMPTION: synthesis, workup and purification are upstream and out of scope; each 96-well product plate enters the cell ready for QC sampling.
ASSUMPTION (conservative): all 8 plates (8 x 96 = 768 products) are available only once the last reaction finishes, so the full QC must fit within 24 h.
ASSUMPTION: screening is a 96-well fluorescence assay with a 1 h incubation, one assay plate per product plate; no reformatting to 384/1536.
ASSUMPTION: room is 7 m x 5 m with a door at x=0, y=2.5. Not supplied by the user.
ASSUMPTION: the cell runs unattended 24 h/day with one technician on an 8 h day shift for loading and replenishment.
Budget unknown: this is a provisional design; the Waters LC-MS is already owned, so its price is not new spend.
Hazards: LC-MS mobile phases and DMSO are flammable solvents. The LC-MS needs a ventilated zone and solvent/waste storage separated from the cell. Not safety certified.
Revision 1: second UR5e arm so transfers from liquid handler to LC-MS do not depend on the 8 h operator shift.
Revision 2: adds a second LC-MS (Agilent 1290/LC-MSD iQ) in parallel; this departs from the user's one-instrument constraint and is shown as the option needed to approach the target.

# Library QC cell: one Waters LC-MS can't QC all 768 products within 24 hours in this model

With no more input available, I made a provisional design under the assumptions below. The model doesn't support the 24-hour target with your one Waters LC-MS, and none of my three designs reached it. These are simulation predictions, not measured performance.

## Assumptions (none came from you)
- **Scope:** synthesis, workup and purification happen before this cell. Each 96-well product plate arrives ready to sample. 8 plates × 96 = 768 products.
- **Timing (cautious case):** all 8 plates become available only when the last reaction finishes, so the whole QC must fit in 24 hours. The target is therefore 768 products/day, running 24 hours a day.
- **LC-MS method:** about 210 s per sample (range 120–360 s), so 20,160 s per plate, with no blanks or standards counted.
  - This is the catalog's estimate, not a vendor or measured figure.
  - The literature search found no library-QC cycle time I could cite. The closest result was a 4-minute run time in a serum bioanalysis paper (doi:10.1016/j.jpba.2024.116179), which is a different application, so I didn't use it.
- **Screening:** a 96-well fluorescence assay with a 1-hour incubation (a placeholder).
- **Room:** 7 × 5 m with one door.
- **Staff:** one technician on an 8-hour day shift.
- **Hazards:** flammable solvents and toxic reagents; the LC-MS sits in a ventilated zone.
- **Budget:** unknown, so the design is provisional.

## Design and results
The cell has input and output plate hotels and an Opentrons Flex. The Flex makes a QC plate and an assay plate from each product plate. QC plates go to the LC-MS; assay plates go through a PlateLoc sealer, a Cytomat incubator and a CLARIOstar reader, then to data review. UR5e arms move the plates.

| Version | Change | Throughput (products/day): P10 / P50 / P90 | Chance of meeting target | What limits it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | Baseline, Waters only, one arm | 146 / 192 / 192 | 0 | The liquid handler is out of the arm's reach, so the technician carries plates to the LC-MS during the day shift only. Waters busy 48% of the time. |
| v2 | Add a second UR5e arm | 280 / **384** / 498 | 0 | **The Waters is busy 99.9% of the time.** It is the hard limit. |
| v3 | Add an Agilent 1290/MSD iQ as a second LC-MS | 263 / 384 / 384 | 0 | The layout put both LC-MS units out of the arms' reach, so the technician has to load them. Each runs about 48% of the time. |

**v2 is the real answer to your question.** With one Waters running non-stop, the model's median is 384 products/day, half the target. At that rate the 768 products take about two days.

The target needs about 112.5 s per sample or less, all-in. Even the fastest end of the estimate (120 s) is too slow before adding blanks or standards.

v3 was my last allowed revision, and it didn't show that two instruments are enough. In the design, the second LC-MS has no robot feeding it overnight.

Simple arithmetic (not a simulation): two LC-MS units fed around the clock at 20,160 s per plate give a ceiling of about 823 products/day. That would only just clear the target at the central estimate and would fail at the slow end. Two-instrument feasibility is unproven.

## Checked claims
- **"P50 meets 768 products/day": refuted.** The verifier recomputed 384. I withdraw any suggestion that this design meets the target.
- **"Zero layout violations": refuted.** There is 1 violation: people hand plates into arm_2's reach at the liquid handler and output hotel, and the UR5e isn't rated for working beside people. A light curtain or a pass-through hotel would fix this, but neither is in the catalog. They're priced only as a placeholder of about $4k.
- No budget was given, so cost wasn't checked against one.

## Cost (catalog estimates, excluding installation, service and consumables)
- **v3 equipment list:** $611,352, including the Waters you already own ($156,700). That makes new spend about **$454,652**.
- **v2 (Waters only, two arms):** new spend about **$240,468**.

## What would change the answer
1. **Plates finishing one after another:** if plates finish in sequence, QC on early plates can start before the last reaction ends. Only the tail end would then need to fit in the 24 hours, and the target could be reachable with one instrument. This is the biggest unknown.
2. **A measured cycle time:** a real sample-to-sample time well under about 112 s, including blanks, would make one Waters possible in principle.
3. **A second LC-MS:** it would need to sit inside an arm's reach, with that arm's 24-hour operation simulated before you commit.

The report I generated matches these findings. Nothing here is a safety certification.

items.title: High-throughput quantification for a drug mixture in rat plasma-a comparison of Ultra Performance liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry with high-performance liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry
items.abstract: A quantitative Ultra Performance liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (UPL/MS/MS) protocol was developed for a five-compound mixture in rat plasma. A similar high-performance liquid chromatography/tandem mass spectrometry (HPLC/MS/MS) quantification protocol was developed for comparison purposes. Among the five test compounds, three preferred positive electrospray ionization (ESI) and two preferred negative ESI. As a result, both UPLC/MS/MS and HPLC/MS/MS analyses were performed by having the mass spectrometer collecting ESI multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) data in both positive and negative ion modes during a single injection. Peak widths for most standards were 4.8 s for the HPLC analysis and 2.4 s for the UPLC analysis. There were 17 to 20 data points obtained for each of the LC peaks. Compared with the HPLC/MS/MS method, the UPLC/MS/MS method offered 3-fold decrease in retention time, up to 10-fold increase in detected peak height, with 2-fold decrease in peak width. Limits of quantification (LOQs) for both HPLC and UPLC methods were evaluated. For UPLC/MS/MS analysis, a linear range up to four orders of magnitude was obtained with r2 values ranging from 0.991 to 0.998. The LOQs for the five analytes ranged from 0.08 to 9.85 ng/mL. Three levels of quality control (QC) samples were analyzed. For the UPLC/MS/MS protocol, the percent relative standard deviation (RSD%) for low QC (2 ng/mL) ranged from 3.42 to 8.67% (N = 18). The carryover of the UPLC/MS/MS protocol was negligible and the robustness of the UPLC/MS/MS system was evaluated with up to 963 QC injections.

items.title: Multiplex enzyme assay for galactosemia using ultraperformance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry
items.abstract:
BACKGROUND: 
Galactosemia is one of the most important inherited disorders detected by newborn screening tests. Abnormal results in screening tests should be confirmed by enzyme activity assays, but existing methods are time and labor intensive. We developed a novel multiplex enzyme assay for galactosemia using ultraperformance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS).
METHODS: 
[(13)C6]-galactose, [(13)C2]-galactose-1-phosphate, and UDP-glucose were used as substrates for 3 galactose-metabolizing enzymes. The end products from the combined reaction mixtures, [(13)C6]-galactose-1-phosphate, UDP-[(13)C2]-galactose, and UDP-galactose, were simultaneously measured using UPLC-MS/MS. Linearity, imprecision, ion suppression, and the effects of substrate were evaluated to determine assay performance. Enzyme activities from 35 healthy individuals, 8 patients with enzyme deficiency, and 18 mutant cells were analyzed.
RESULTS: 
Substrates, products, and internal standards from the mixture of 3 enzyme reactions were clearly separated by using UPLC-MS/MS, with an injection cycle time of 10 min. Ion suppression was 0.1%-2.5%, the interassay imprecision of UPLC-MS/MS was 3.3%-10.6% CV, and the linearity of each system was good (R(2) = 0.994-0.999). Patient samples and mutated cells showed consistently low enzyme activities compared with those of normal individuals and wild-type cells.
CONCLUSIONS: 
This method allows for a high-throughput and reproducible multiplex enzyme assay for galactosemia in erythrocytes.

items.title: Acoustic Ejection/Full-Scan Mass Spectrometry Analysis for High-Throughput Compound Quality Control
items.abstract: High-throughput analysis of compound dissolved in DMSO and arrayed in multiwell plates for quality control (QC) purposes has widespread utility in drug discovery, ranging from the QC of assay-ready plates dispatched by compound management, to compound integrity check in the screening collection, to reaction monitoring of chemical syntheses in microtiter plates. Due to the large number of samples (thousands per batch) involved, these workflows can put a significant burden on the liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) platform typically used. To achieve the required speed of seconds per sample, several chromatography-free MS approaches have previously been used with mixed results. In this study, we demonstrated the feasibility of acoustic ejection-mass spectrometry (AE-MS) in full-scan mode for high-throughput compound QC in miniaturized formats, featuring direct, contactless liquid sampling, minimal sample consumption, and ultrafast analytical speed. The sample consumption and analysis time by AE-MS represent, respectively, a 1000-fold and 30-fold reduction compared with LC-MS. In qualitative QC, AE-MS generated comparable results to conventional LC-MS in identifying the presence and absence of expected compounds. AE-MS also demonstrated its utility in relative quantifications of the same compound in serial dilution plates, or substrate in chemical synthesis. To facilitate the processing of a large amount of data generated by AE-MS, we have developed a data processing platform using commercially available tools. The platform demonstrated fast and straightforward data extraction, reviewing, and reporting, thus eliminating the need for the development of custom data processing tools. The overall AE-MS workflow has effectively eliminated the analytical bottleneck in the high-throughput compound QC work stream.

items.title: Establishing Quality Control Procedures for Large-Scale Plasma Proteomics Analyses
items.abstract: Proteomics research has been transformed due to high-throughput liquid chromatography (LC-MS/MS) tandem mass spectrometry instruments combined with highly sophisticated automated sample preparation and multiplexing workflows. However, scaling proteomics experiments to large sample cohorts (hundreds to thousands) requires thoughtful quality control (QC) protocols. Robust QC protocols can help with reproducibility, quantitative accuracy, and provide opportunities for more decisive troubleshooting. Our laboratory conducted a plasma proteomics study of a cohort of N = 335 patient samples using tandem mass tag (TMTpro) 16-plex batches. Over the course of a 10-month data acquisition period for this cohort we collected 271 pooled QC LC-MS/MS result files obtained from MS/MS analysis of a patient-derived pooled plasma sample, representative of the entire cohort population. This sample was tagged with TMTzero or TMTpro reagents and used to inform the daily performance of the LC-MS/MS instruments and to allow within and across sample batch normalization. Analytical variability of a number of instrumental and data analysis metrics including protein and peptide identifications, peptide spectral matches (PSMs), number of obtained MS/MS spectra, average peptide abundance, percent of peptides with a Δ m/z between ±0.003 Da, percent of MS/MS spectra obtained at the maximum injection time, and the retention time of selected tracking peptides were evaluated to help inform the design of a robust LC-MS/MS QC workflow for use in future cohort studies. This study also led to general tips for using selected metrics to inform real-time troubleshooting of LC-MS/MS performance issues with daily QC checks.

items.abstract: A sensitive, reproducible, robust, high-throughput ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) method was developed and validated for the simultaneous quantification of fexofenadine and olmesartan in human serum. Samples (50 μL) undergo protein precipitation prior to UPLC-MS/MS analysis. The analytes were separated using an Acquity BEH C18 column (2.1 mm × 50 mm, 1.7 μm) at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min using a gradient elution with a total run time of 4 min. The analytes were detected in positive ion mode and selected reaction monitoring (SRM) was used for quantitation. The standard curve concentration range was 1.0-500.0 ng/mL for both analytes and each analyte showed excellent linearity with correlation coefficients (R2 > 0.99). The intra- and inter-day accuracy and precision were ±15% for each analyte, and excellent recovery was demonstrated (93-98%) for both analytes. The method is well suited for high-throughput quantitative determination of fexofenadine and olmesartan simultaneously and was successfully applied to an in vivo pharmacokinetic and transporter phenotyping study in humans.
